> **In development.** This article shows the API planned for zuroar
> 0.1.0. The functions are not available yet, and the output shown is
> the output the design specifies.

zuroar gives R compressed sets of whole numbers. A bitmap holds values
from 0 to 2^32 - 1, stores dense stretches and long runs in a fraction of
the memory a plain vector needs, and answers membership, counts and set
operations without expanding them. To R code it looks like a sorted
vector without duplicates. Bitmaps are written in the portable Roaring
format, so Python, Java, Go and Rust programs can read them.

```{r}
library(zuroar)
```

## Building a bitmap

`roar()` takes integer or whole-number double values. Order and
duplicates don't matter: a bitmap is a set.

```{r}
mon <- roar(c(42, 3, 99, 8, 15, 8))
length(mon)
#> [1] 5
as.double(mon)
#> [1]  3  8 15 42 99
```

`roar_range()` builds every value between two ends, both included, as
`seq()` does. A million consecutive values compress to a few run
containers.

```{r}
y <- roar_range(1, 1e6)
length(y)
#> [1] 1e+06
```

`roar_add()` and `roar_remove()` take values, or a range through `from`
and `to`. Like every zuroar function, they return a new bitmap and leave
their argument unchanged.

```{r}
y <- roar_remove(y, from = 10, to = 19)
y <- roar_add(y, from = 2e6, to = 3e6)
length(y)
#> [1] 1999991
```

## A sorted vector without duplicates

Wherever R allows it, a bitmap behaves like `sort(unique(v))`. Positions
count from 1, and `[` returns a bitmap, the way it keeps the class of a
`Date`.

```{r}
mon[[2]]
#> [1] 8
as.double(mon[2:3])
#> [1]  8 15
as.double(mon[-1])
#> [1]  8 15 42 99
as.double(head(mon, 2))
#> [1] 3 8
as.double(tail(mon, 1))
#> [1] 99
```

`c()` is the union, and adding or subtracting a number shifts every
value.

```{r}
as.double(c(mon, roar(c(1, 100))))
#> [1]   1   3   8  15  42  99 100
as.double(mon + 10)
#> [1]  13  18  25  52 109
```

A shift that would push a value below 0 or above 2^32 - 1 is an error,
so values never disappear silently. Ask for that explicitly with
`drop = TRUE`.

```{r}
mon - 5            # an error: 3 - 5 is below 0
as.double(roar_shift(mon, by = -5, drop = TRUE))
#> [1]  3 10 37 94
```

Where the vector meaning and the set meaning disagree, zuroar refuses
rather than guess: `rev(mon)`, `mon[1] <- 5` and `mon > 10` are errors.
To loop over the values, convert first: `for (v in as.double(mon))`.

## Membership and queries

`roar_contains()` is the fast membership test. `%in%` gives the same
answer but expands the bitmap into a vector first.

```{r}
roar_contains(mon, c(8, 9))
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE
8 %in% mon
#> [1] TRUE
min(mon)
#> [1] 3
max(mon)
#> [1] 99
```

Ranges are inclusive at both ends. `roar_count()` counts the values in a
range; `roar_contains_range()` asks whether all of them are present.

```{r}
roar_count(y, from = 1, to = 20)
#> [1] 10
roar_contains_range(y, from = 1, to = 9)
#> [1] TRUE
roar_contains_range(y, from = 1, to = 10)
#> [1] FALSE
```

`roar_rank()` counts the values at or below `v`, and `roar_select()` is
its inverse: the `k`-th smallest value, counting from 1. `roar_next()`
and `roar_prev()` find the nearest value on either side, and give `NA`
when there is none.

```{r}
roar_rank(y, 25)
#> [1] 15
roar_select(y, 15)
#> [1] 25
roar_next(y, c(10, 30))
#> [1] 20 30
roar_prev(y, 10)
#> [1] 9
roar_next(mon, 100)
#> [1] NA
```

`roar_values()` extracts a bounded slice without expanding the rest.

```{r}
roar_values(y, from = 999998, n = 4)
#> [1]  999998  999999 1000000 2000000
```

## Set algebra

Between two bitmaps, `|` is the union and `&` the intersection.
`roar_andnot()` is the difference and `roar_xor()` the symmetric
difference.

```{r}
tue <- roar(c(8, 15, 16, 23, 42))

as.double(mon | tue)
#> [1]  3  8 15 16 23 42 99
as.double(mon & tue)
#> [1]  8 15 42
as.double(roar_andnot(mon, tue))
#> [1]  3 99
as.double(roar_xor(mon, tue))
#> [1]  3 16 23 99
```

`roar_union()` and `roar_intersect()` take any number of bitmaps.

```{r}
wed <- roar(c(8, 42, 50))
as.double(roar_intersect(mon, tue, wed))
#> [1]  8 42
```

Comparisons are about sets: `==` is equality, `<=` subset and `<` strict
subset.

```{r}
(mon & tue) <= mon
#> [1] TRUE
mon < mon
#> [1] FALSE
```

When only a number is needed, no bitmap is built at all.

```{r}
roar_cardinality(mon, tue, op = "and")
#> [1] 3
roar_jaccard(mon, tue)
#> [1] 0.4285714
roar_intersects(mon, tue)
#> [1] TRUE
roar_disjoint(mon, roar(c(1, 2)))
#> [1] TRUE
```

`roar_flip()` complements a bitmap within a range.

```{r}
as.double(roar_flip(roar(c(1, 2, 5)), from = 0, to = 5))
#> [1] 0 3 4
```

## Exact values

Values are never silently changed. `as.double()` is exact over the whole
domain; `as.integer()` is an error rather than `NA` for values above
`.Machine$integer.max`.

```{r}
big <- roar(c(0, 2^31, 2^32 - 1))
as.double(big)
#> [1]          0 2147483648 4294967295
as.integer(big)    # an error: 2^31 is above .Machine$integer.max
```

Input outside the domain is an error of class `zuroar_error_value`, which
names the first offending position. A logical vector is refused too: use
`which()` to say which positions you mean.

```{r}
roar(c(1, -1))     # an error naming element 2
keep <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
as.double(roar(which(keep)))
#> [1] 1 3
```

## Compression

`roar_optimize()` converts long runs to run containers. `roar_size()`
reports the bytes the bitmap uses, and `roar_stats()` which kinds of
container hold the values.

```{r}
y <- roar_optimize(y)
roar_size(y)
roar_stats(y)
```

The benchmarks article compares memory and speed with base R and the
bit package.

## 64-bit bitmaps

`roar64()` builds a bitmap over 0 to 2^64 - 1. R has no exact 64-bit
integer, so values go in and come out as decimal text, or as doubles
below 2^53.

```{r}
z <- roar64(c("0", "18446744073709551615"))
length(z)
#> [1] 2
as.character(z)
#> [1] "0"                    "18446744073709551615"
```

Counts are doubles too, and `length()` is an error if one exceeds 2^53.
`roar64_length()` always gives the count exactly, as text.

```{r}
roar64_length(z)
#> [1] "2"
```

## Saving and sharing

`roar_serialize()` writes the portable Roaring format as a raw vector.
`roar_unserialize()` reads it back, checking untrusted bytes before using
them, and `roar64_unserialize()` reads the 64-bit format.

```{r}
bytes <- roar_serialize(mon)
roar_unserialize(bytes) == mon
#> [1] TRUE
roar64_unserialize(roar_serialize(z)) == z
#> [1] TRUE
```

The same bytes can be read by pyroaring's `BitMap.deserialize()`, Java's
RoaringBitmap and the other Roaring implementations.

A bitmap lives outside R's memory, so `saveRDS()` alone doesn't keep it:
save `roar_serialize(x)` instead. For parallel work with mirai,
`roar_serial_config()` lets bitmaps travel to workers and back.

```{r}
library(mirai)
daemons(2, serial = roar_serial_config())
m <- mirai(length(x), x = mon)
m[]
#> [1] 5
daemons(0)
```

## Where next

`zuroar_info()` reports the CRoaring version and which processor
instructions the running build uses. The reference pages document every
function.
